newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. tribunal resumes Rwanda genocide trial.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tribunal resumes Rwanda genocide trial.

text.p: The trial resumed on Tuesday of Rwandan Georges Rutaganda, a militia vice-president accused of genocide in Rwanda in 1994, at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
His trial was suspended early in April after the prosecution failed to inform the defence in advance of the name of its next witness. Witnesses are not named in public to protect their identify.
Rutaganda, a former businessman and vice-president of a militia, sat in court in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Tuesday as a witness identified only as "DD" testified.
The witness said he saw Rutaganda with troops and militiamen of the extremist Hutu Interahamwe militia at the entrance of a technical school where thousands of Tutsis were attacked in 1994.
Rutaganda's trial started in March. Lawyers defending another accused on Monday asked the tribunal to dismiss the case against him, arguing it had no jurisdiction to put him on trial.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was modelled on the Hague-based criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, which was set up by the U.N. Security Council in 1993 and was the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
The Rwanda U.N. tribunal has been plagued by problems in attempting to bring to justice the leaders of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
So far 21 people have been indicted by the Rwanda tribunal, which has a total of 12 suspects in detention in Arusha.
